paper_title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) represent model activations with sparse, linearly decoded features, but the downstream effects of those features need not compose additively. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR), which measure the behavioral variation left unexplained above a chosen interaction order. Under independent feature subset sampling, population SAR is exactly the normalized energy of interactions above that order and bounds coalition ordering error for the optimal low order approximation. To distinguish compositionality associated with the SAE representation from that induced by downstream computation, we compare learned SAE coordinates with sum preserving random rotations of the same selected subspace and find lower first order residuals for the learned coordinates across all 18 model and behavior settings. The coordinates are nevertheless not fully additive: pairwise terms improve held out coalition ordering in every setting and outperform parameter matched models using randomly selected third order terms. In a combined steering experiment, pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. Together, these results show that SAE coordinates support comparatively compositional behavioral descriptions while faithful joint explanations and interventions still require interactions beyond individual feature effects. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/SAE-Behavioral-Compositionality.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose model activations into sparse, linearly decoded features. These coordinates are used to inspect computation, build multi-feature explanations, and manipulate behavior. This raises basic question. If the effects of individual features are known, can their joint effect be predicted by summing them? linear SAE decoder does not answer this because subsequent computation can make feature effects reinforce, suppress, or depend on one another. This matters when SAE features are combined into circuits, joint explanations, or interventions (Marks et al., 2025; Ameisen et al., 2025; Ayonrinde et al., 2024). Existing SAE evaluations characterize reconstruction, sparsity, and interpretability (Karvonen et al., 2025; Engels et al., 2025b; Chanin et al., 2025; Engels et al., 2025a), but do not tell us when independently characterized features can be composed into faithful joint explanations or interventions. To address this gap, we introduce framework for measuring behavioral compositionality in SAE coordinates. For each prompt, we retain different subsets of selected decoded contributions while holding the remaining activation fixed, producing downstream response over feature subsets. If individual feature effects compose faithfully, this response should be well described at first order. Departures from that approximation reveal interaction, and adding successively higher interaction orders shows how that missing structure is organized. (b, c) Nearly additive and interacting responses, showing the first order fit, pairwise interactions, and variance decomposition. SAR1 is the residual beyond individual features and ρ2 = 2/SAR1 its pairwise share. these interventions depends on coordinate choice beyond the subspace and downstream continuation and whether the remaining interaction matters for explanation and steering. 2 = SAR1 SAR2 is the structure recovered by pairs and ρ2 = We quantify this structure with SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR). At first order, SAR1 is the behavioral variation not explained by individual feature effects. Adding pairs gives SAR2, so 2/SAR1 its share of the first order residual. Under independent subset sampling, SAR has an exact interaction decomposition so that residual structure above given order is exactly the normalized energy of higher order interactions. The same quantity also controls errors in preserving the ordering of feature coalitions. Figure 1 illustrates the intervention and contrasts nearly additive and interacting responses. The main experiments span three model and SAE pipelines and six behavioral readouts, with additional analyses across seven pipelines and multiple representation depths. We evaluate matched coordinate rotations, first order and pairwise coalition models, combined SAE steering directions, and reconstruction quality. Our contributions are: We formulate behavioral compositionality for SAE representations and connect low order approximation error to explicit feature interactions and coalition ordering. Using sum preserving rotations of the same selected activation subspace, we show that compositionality under the subset intervention depends on coordinate choice, with learned SAE coordinates supporting lower order behavioral description than the tested rotations. We show that pairwise terms improve held out coalition ordering in each of the 18 tested settings and outperform parameter matched random third order controls. We extend the analysis to combined SAE steering experiment, where pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790, and find that SAR and reconstruction quality differ in matched six SAE comparison.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: SAE evaluation commonly measures reconstruction, sparsity, interpretability, and downstream utility (Karvonen et al., 2025). Reconstruction residuals retain structure, concepts can be absorbed across latents, and some model features require multidimensional descriptions (Engels et al., 2025b; Chanin et al., 2025; Engels et al., 2025a). Polynomial SAEs add explicit higher order decoder terms (Koromilas et al., 2026). These works characterize SAE representations and reconstruction, but not whether fixed SAE coordinates compose behaviorally after their decoded contributions pass through the remaining model. Work on multi-feature explanations includes independent additivity (Ayonrinde et al., 2024), attribution graphs and feature circuits (Ameisen et al., 2025; Marks et al., 2025), and interventions on internal components (Wang et al., 2023; Conmy et al., 2023; Hanna et al., 2024; Kramár et al., 2024). Because circuits, joint explanations, and interventions combine multiple components, individual characterization does not establish that their effects admit faithful low order joint description. This motivates measuring compositionality directly in the downstream response. Interaction indices study joint effects among multiple players (Lundberg & Lee, 2017; Sundararajan et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2023; Bordt & von Luxburg, 2023). SAEs provide structured setting in which the players are learned sparse features intended to separate activation structure into interpretable coordinates. We study the interaction that remains when these coordinates are combined downstream and how it is distributed across orders. Appendix gives the relation to interaction indices and coalition weighting.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We first characterize compositionality across behaviors and representations, then compare learned coordinates with matched random rotations and test whether pairwise structure recovers failures of first order explanations. We finally examine depth, combined steering directions, and the relation to reconstruction quality. The main comparisons use Gemma-3 4B, Mistral-7B, and Llama-3.1 8B across simple copying, subject verb agreement, gendered pronoun preference, CounterFact (Meng et al., 2022), IOI (Wang et al., 2023), and greater than comparison. The fixed layer landscape, rotation, fidelity, and pairwise analyses use 1,000, 100, 800, and 150 prompts per model and behavior setting, respectively. For each prompt, we select the top = 16 active SAE contributions and sample 384 coalitions, using 256 for fitting and 128 for evaluation. Appendix gives the full model, behavior, and sampling specifications. 4.1 Behavioral compositionality varies across behaviors and representations We first ask whether first order additivity is reasonable approximation across behaviors and representations. The prompt median (cid:100)SAR1 is positive in all 57 model, layer, and behavior combinations while affine controls remain at numerical zero. Its magnitude also varies across settings. Simple copying and subject verb agreement have lower residuals than CounterFact in all three main pipelines, while the other behaviors change order across models. Thus first order additivity is not exact in these intervention games, and the estimated residual varies with both behavior and representation. 6 Figure 2: Prompt median (cid:100)SAR1 for six behaviors in Gemma-3 4B layer 22, Mistral-7B layer 24, and Llama-3.1 8B layer 21. Error bars show 95% prompt bootstrap intervals. Figure 3: Paired first order SAR for learned SAE coordinates and sum preserving random rotations of the same selected activation subspace. 4.2 Compositionality depends on coordinate choice under subset interventions We compare each SAE basis with sum preserving rotations of the same selected subspace to test whether compositionality under the subset intervention depends on coordinate choice rather than only on the subspace and downstream continuation. Figure 3 shows the paired comparison for all 18 model and behavior combinations. Learned SAE coordinates have lower median (cid:100)SAR1 in every comparison, although the size of the gap varies across settings. For example, the medians are 0.0218 and 0.1196 for Mistral subject verb agreement. The selected subspace, total contribution, and downstream continuation remain fixed as the intervention coordinates change. The systematic SAR gap therefore shows that, under this intervention, these shared factors alone do not determine compositionality; the learned SAE basis supports lower order description than the tested rotations. Under milder interventions, pairwise rank improvement persists at = 0.75, while halving removed contributions lowers (cid:100)SAR1 and improves first order rank fidelity in eight of nine settings. Appendix gives the full controls. 4.3 Estimated SAR is associated with first order coalition fidelity The ordering theorem bounds the population behavior weighted ordering error. As descriptive calibration, we compare estimated SAR with rank fidelity and selection regret on the same held out coalitions. Figure 4 shows lower rank fidelity and higher selection regret from the lowest to the highest (cid:100)SAR1 decile in all three models. Selection regret approximately doubles in Gemma and Llama and increases by about fivefold in Mistral. Across 18 model and behavior combinations, the prompt level correlation between (cid:100)SAR1 and rank fidelity is negative in 17 and at most 0.6 in 14. 4.4 Feature pairs recover missing coalition structure The previous results identify settings where individual feature effects are insufficient. We therefore ask how much of the missing structure can be recovered by the next interaction 7 Figure 4: First order explanation fidelity across (cid:100)SAR1 deciles within each model. Figure 5 shows the paired comparison between first order and pairwise approximations across all 18 model and behavior combinations. Pairwise models improve rank fidelity in all 18 model and behavior combinations, raising the average from 0.9782 to 0.9959, and satisfy (cid:98)E2 < (cid:98)E1 in all 18. Both improvements persist across all 20 repeated fitting and evaluation splits. Selection regret falls from 0.0272 to 0.0051 on average, and sign error also decreases in every combination. These results show that pairwise terms capture substantial predictive structure beyond individual feature effects. Pairwise models have higher held out rank fidelity and lower behavior weighted ordering error than the median matched model in all 18 combinations. The full comparison is in Appendix H.4. 4.5 Estimated compositionality varies across depth We next examine how the estimated compositionality measures change across representation depth. Figure 6 follows simple copying, CounterFact, and IOI. Across nine early to late comparisons, (cid:100)SAR1 decreases in eight and (cid:98)ρ2 increases in all nine. Later representations therefore usually have lower estimated first order residuals, while (cid:98)ρ2 increases. This may reflect either the SAE coordinates or the shorter remaining downstream computation. Random rotations show the same first order decrease in eight of nine comparisons, indicating that part of the depth trend comes from the remaining downstream computation rather than the SAE basis. SAE coordinates nevertheless have lower (cid:100)SAR1 than rotations in all 33 model, behavior, and layer comparisons. Thus part of the depth trend is shared across coordinate systems, while SAE coordinates remain lower residual than rotations at matched sites; (cid:98)ρ2 also increases. The Llama profiles are nonmonotonic near the final sampled layer. 8 Figure 6: Depth profiles for simple copying, CounterFact, and IOI. Across all seven pipelines, simple copying has lower (cid:100)SAR1 at the latest sampled representation in six cases and higher (cid:98)ρ2 in all seven. The pattern therefore extends beyond the three main pipelines. Appendix Figure 7 and Table 13 give the full comparison. 4.6 Pairwise modeling better predicts the aggregate steering response The preceding experiments study interactions among feature contributions already present in model activation. SAE features are also used by adding directions to steer model behavior. If these effects compose poorly, effects measured for individual steering directions may not predict the outcome of combining them. We therefore apply the same analysis to fixed published steering directions. Using 16 published CorrSteer features (Cho et al., 2026) in Llama-3.1 8B, we evaluate 1,024 steering combinations with separate fitting and evaluation coalitions. sections.title: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: Linear decoding makes SAE coordinates additive for activation reconstruction, not for downstream effects. Reconstruction quality, individual feature interpretability, and the interaction order needed for joint behavior are therefore distinct representation properties, with SAR measuring the last directly. This matters whenever SAE features are combined: meaningful individual coordinates need not have additive joint behavioral effects. Learned SAE coordinates nevertheless have lower first order residuals than the tested sum preserving random rotations of the same selected contribution subspaces. Individual effects remain insufficient in many cases, while pairwise terms improve coalition prediction. The SAE basis therefore supports lower order description than these rotations without making feature effects independent, so residual interaction can matter for faithful joint explanations. The distinction also appears in steering and differs from reconstruction quality in the matched SAE comparison. These conclusions depend on the selected contributions, behavioral readout, and intervention distribution rather than global property of an SAE dictionary. Behavioral compositionality is therefore distinct property to consider when SAE features are combined for explanation or intervention.

sections.title: C Interaction Indices and Alternative Constructions
sections.content: C.1 Interaction indices and low order fits Interaction indices extend feature attribution from individual players to small coalitions. The Shapley value assigns each player weighted average of its marginal contributions (Shapley, 1953), and its extensions assign values to pairs and larger subsets (Grabisch & Roubens, 1999; Sundararajan et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2023). Several such quantities can be interpreted as coefficients of low order fits (Lundberg & Lee, 2017; Tsai et al., 2023; Bordt & von Luxburg, 2023). SAR instead aggregates the residual energy that remains above chosen order. Under product sampling with = 1/2, the relation to pairwise interactions is explicit. Theorem 1 gives (47) c{i,j} = 1 SN{i,j}[ 16 ijg(S)]. Thus the pairwise Fourier coefficient is scaled context averaged second finite difference. The quantity 2 aggregates the squared pairwise coefficients rather than assigning an individual importance score to each pair. Low order coefficients alone do not determine the residual above that order. Under the product measure, the basis terms with and > occupy orthogonal subspaces. Changing the latter leaves every fitted coefficient up to order unchanged while changing SARr. Estimating the residual therefore requires behavioral evaluations beyond the fitted coefficients themselves, which is why the estimator uses separate evaluation split. C.2 Coalition weighting and variance shares The weighting that makes first order fit reproduce the Shapley value places weight proportional to [( S)S(K S)]1 on nontrivial coalitions (Lundberg & Lee, 2017). This weighting correlates feature memberships, so the product basis used in Theorem 1 is no longer orthogonal. The differences in the SAR sequence therefore do not have the same variance share interpretation under that weighting. Product sampling gives independent memberships and the orthogonal decomposition used here. The two weightings answer different questions. C.3 Alternative intervention games natural alternative to Equation (2) reconstructs the activation from the retained subset alone, h(S) = iS δi(x). This discards the reconstruction residual and the features outside the selected set. The full coalition then evaluates the behavior of the SAE reconstruction rather than the original model activation. The discarded component can also carry structure and behavioral effect (Engels et al., 2025b). Equation (2) keeps this component fixed, anchors the full coalition at hx, and makes comparisons across SAE bases refer to the same original activation. C.4 Scope of the zero point The tested states lie in h0 + span{δi(x) Nx}, whose dimension is at most K. continuation can be nonlinear away from this subspace and still induce an additive response on the tested states. Behavioral compositionality therefore concerns the downstream computation expressed in the selected SAE coordinates. This is the coordinate space used when those contributions form joint explanation or intervention.
